Accessible name: The text alternative used to identify an interface element in accessibility APIs, computed from the relevant naming rules and relationships.
Attribute: A name and value associated with an element. Its authoring syntax and behavior depend on its definition and context.
Boolean attribute: An attribute whose defined true state is represented by presence and false state by absence. The string false does not turn it off.
Browsing context: A context in which a document can be presented, such as a top-level page or an embedded iframe, with further terminology defined by the Standard.
Character reference: HTML source syntax that represents a character, such as < for a less-than sign in a relevant parsing context.
Conformance: Satisfaction of the applicable requirements of a specification. A checker result has a version and scope; it is not a general accessibility or security certificate.
Content model: The defined rules for an element's contents, including categories and additional restrictions.
Content category: A classification used by the Standard to describe elements and content rules. Categories can overlap or have conditional membership.
Content attribute: An attribute represented in the markup/DOM attribute layer, distinguished from a corresponding IDL property and current control state.
Custom element: An element defined through the custom-elements machinery. A valid autonomous custom-element name has a required hyphen and other naming restrictions.
Descendant: A node reached by following child relationships one or more levels down the tree. It need not be a direct child.
Document element: The element child of a document; for an ordinary HTML document it is html.
DOM: The document object model: nodes, relationships and APIs through which software can inspect and modify documents.
Enumerated attribute: An attribute defined in terms of keywords and states, potentially with distinct missing-value and invalid-value defaults.
Fallback: An alternative path or representation designed for the actual failure or unsupported case. Its presence does not prove that users can reach or use it.
Flow content: A content category covering much of the material used in a document body. Membership still depends on the individual element definition.
Focus: The platform's designation of an interaction target for relevant input. Focusable and sequentially focusable are related but distinct concepts.
Fragment: The part of a URL introduced by #, commonly used to navigate to a matching id within a document.
Global attribute: An attribute applicable across HTML elements under its defined rules. This does not remove contextual constraints or cross-specification ownership.
Hyperlink: A link to another resource or location, commonly created by an a element with href.
IDL property: A property exposed through a web interface. Reflection can parse or normalize an attribute, and some properties represent live state rather than raw markup.
Inert: A state that suppresses certain interaction and focus behavior and affects accessibility exposure under the relevant platform rules.
Landmark: An accessibility role identifying a useful region for navigation, such as main content or a named navigation area.
Living Standard: A specification maintained over time rather than a single frozen feature release. Its current presence and browser support are separate questions.
Metadata: Information about the document or its relationships, commonly placed in head using elements such as title, meta and link.
Namespace: A mechanism distinguishing vocabularies and names, important at HTML, SVG, MathML and XML integration boundaries.
Origin: A security-relevant identity derived under platform rules, ordinarily involving scheme, host and port for a conventional URL. Opaque origins and special cases exist.
Phrasing content: A category used for text and markup that participates at the phrasing level of a document. Extra element-specific restrictions still apply.
Progressive enhancement: Designing an appropriate useful baseline and adding capabilities without needlessly destroying that baseline when an enhancement fails.
Reflection: The defined relationship between a content attribute and an interface property. It is not a universal raw-string equivalence.
Sandbox: A set of restrictions for an embedded browsing context. Added permission tokens restore capabilities and must be reviewed for the actual trust boundary.
Serialization: A textual representation of a document or fragment. HTML and XML serialization have different rules and processing consequences.
Shadow tree: A DOM tree attached through a shadow root, used for encapsulation and composition. It is not a general security sandbox.
Slot: A placeholder for assigned content in a shadow tree. A slot element and a slot attribute have different jobs.
Text alternative: A textual replacement or representation suited to non-text content's actual purpose and context.
Tokenization: The parsing stage that recognizes tokens according to the tokenizer's state before tree-construction rules process them.
Transparent content model: A model that derives permitted content from the surrounding context while preserving the element's own additional restrictions.
Tree construction: The parsing rules that turn tokens into nodes and relationships, including specified recovery behavior.
Void element: An HTML element that has no contents and no end tag in HTML syntax, such as img or input.
WebVTT: A text format commonly used for timed text tracks. A valid file still needs content review against the actual media.
